title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E410 (Novi Commentarii 15, 1771) first derives the static equations for a planar, inextensible filament that is perfectly flexible or elastic. It then turns statics into dynamics by d'Alembert's principle: each element Mm is treated as acted on by the applied forces plus reversed inertial forces (Sigma/2g) x_tt and (Sigma/2g) y_tt. Here Sigma is the weight per unit length and 2g is Euler's acceleration of gravity, his g being the fall in one second. The previous page resolves these forces along the tangent MT and the normal mr. This page substitutes them for p ds and q ds in the static equations.

The unknowns are tension T(s,t), shear (normal) force V(s,t), lever distance v(s,t) and tangent angle Phi(s,t). Euler's convention is dx/ds = sin Phi and dy/ds = cos Phi, with arc length s as the material coordinate. The system reads:

(I) T_s + V Phi_s = (P + Sigma x_tt/2g) sin Phi + (Q + Sigma y_tt/2g) cos Phi. This is tangential balance.

(II) V_s - T Phi_s = (Q + Sigma y_tt/2g) sin Phi - (P + Sigma x_tt/2g) cos Phi. This is normal balance.

(III) V v = S Phi_s. The bending moment equals the stiffness S(s) times the curvature Phi_s (Euler-Bernoulli law).

(IV) (V v)_s = V. This is moment balance.

Euler remarks that the static ordinary derivatives must now be read as partial derivatives, written with his parenthesis ('clausulae') notation, since all quantities depend on s and t. The absolute elasticity S depends on s alone.

He then sketches the solution strategy. First eliminate T, V and v to get a single equation in t, s, x, y and Phi. Using x_s = sin Phi and y_s = cos Phi, this reduces to one equation in s, t and Phi. It determines Phi(s,t), from which x and y, and hence the figure and motion, follow by quadrature. On the next page he combines III and IV into V = (S Phi_s)_s. He then specializes to the perfectly flexible string (S = 0, so V = 0) with small transverse motion. This recovers the vibrating-string equations of d'Alembert, Euler and Bernoulli.

In modern terms, this is the full geometrically nonlinear planar dynamics of an inextensible Euler-Bernoulli rod (Kirchhoff rod in the plane, with rotatory inertia neglected) under distributed loads.
errors: Equation III as printed/transcribed reads V v = S(dPhi/dt). Consistency with IV and with the next page, V = S Phi_ss + S_s Phi_s, requires Phi_s (dPhi/ds). This is either a misprint in the original or a misreading of the scan.

Gap in the solution sketch: x and y enter only through x_tt and y_tt. Recovering them from Phi requires x = x0(t) + integral of sin Phi ds (similarly for y), so the 'single equation in s, t, Phi' is really integro-differential. The motion of a reference point and the boundary conditions also enter. Euler glosses over this; he admits on the next page that no method is known for treating these intricate formulas.

The signs of the inertial terms (+Sigma/2g x_tt, added to P and Q) follow Euler's convention for the directions XA and MX and for the reversed inertial forces 'applied in the mind'. They are consistent within his scheme, not an error, but they differ from the modern sign layout.

ideas.what: Obtaining the equations of motion of a flexible/elastic line from the static equilibrium equations by adding reversed inertial forces element-wise
ideas.modern_name: d'Alembert's principle applied to a continuum (rod)
ideas.usually_credited_to: d'Alembert (1743); applied to strings by d'Alembert and Euler (1740s)
ideas.where_published: E410 itself; also earlier Euler string papers (e.g. E140) and the general principle in E177

ideas.what: Complete nonlinear planar equations of motion for an inextensible elastic rod with tension, shear force and bending moment proportional to curvature
ideas.modern_name: Dynamic planar Kirchhoff/Euler elastica (geometrically exact inextensible beam) equations
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E410, 1771), as analyzed by Truesdell; the 3D theory to Kirchhoff (1859)
ideas.where_published: E410, Novi Comm. Acad. Petrop. 15 (1771); discussed in Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies 1638-1788 (Opera Omnia II 11.2)

ideas.what: Explicit remark that functions of one variable become functions of two, requiring partial-derivative ('clausula') notation
ideas.where_published: Numerous Euler works from the 1750s on, e.g. the fluid mechanics papers E225-E227

ideas.what: Strategy of reducing the system to a single equation for the tangent angle Phi(s,t)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler; used in modern rod theory

deep.surprise_reason: The page states the general dynamic equations of the elastic line, which Truesdell's Opera Omnia commentary already identifies and credits to Euler. The solution strategy is only a sketch, and Euler himself flags it as intractable. Nothing beyond a probable misprint (dt for ds in III) seems absent from the record.
transcription_corrections: III: 'S(dPhi/dt)' should mathematically be 'S(dPhi/ds)'. Check the scan: either it is a misprint in the original or a misreading; the next page's V = S Phi_ss + S_s Phi_s confirms ds.
'functionem esse ipsius S tantum' should read 'ipsius s tantum' (a function of arc length s only).
